utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, if I could address you on behalf of all counsel, the position today is that Judge Cassese is ill. As I hope you've been informed, he is indisposed and won't be with us for the rest of the week. Having had notification of this, what we propose is this, that in order not to delay the trial unnecessarily and not to waste time, we propose to hear evidence of any witness who is here by way of deposition. This is the practice which has been followed by another Trial Chamber in the case of Blaskic on a number of occasions when one of the Trial Chamber has been ill. There is a power under Rule 77 to hear deposition evidence, and the effect is this, that in exceptional circumstances, the Trial Chamber, looking at Rule 71, at the request of either party and in the interests of justice may order that a deposition be taken for use at trial, and the Rule says "... appoint for that purpose a presiding officer." The practice which is being followed is, in fact, the same as during the course of the trial. So the evidence is taken in the normal way, except that only two of the Judges are present, and so there would be examination of the witness, cross-examination, and re-examination. A record would be made by means of the transcript and, of course, a video recording, which would enable the third Judge to view the proceedings. Now, this appears to be an expeditious way to deal with the matter, but, of course, it's subject to the agreement and consent of the parties. I would add that there's been a further development which is that we've been told that two of the witnesses who it was intended to call are, in fact, snowbound in Sarajevo. We were told that it might be possible to get them here today but by no means certain. Because there were a number of people involved and the necessary arrangements had to be made, we decided that it was better not to try and bring them here in rather difficult circumstances, and we've so advised the Victims and Witnesses Unit, but there is a third or one other witness. You will see from Rule 71 that the matter can only be put in hand by request of a party, but I hope that might be forthcoming, that a presiding officer must be appointed. The presiding officers for this purpose would be the two Judges present, and what is proposed is that, in effect, the evidence would be given in the normal way, save that there would only be two Judges present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Prosecution also wishes that this trial not be delayed in any way, and we are in agreement with the proposal made by this Trial Chamber to proceed today and perhaps tomorrow under Rule 71.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, could I take that as a request by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr. President. This, indeed, is a request, a motion, put forward by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It would, of course, be limited now to one witness who is the witness who's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe perhaps this is a good time to raise this issue. Yesterday, we received notice that there would possibly be a second witness, Mr. Blaz. I'm not sure whether this person has arrived in The Hague today and whether this person is available to testify or is, perhaps, on the way. Perhaps the Defence can clarify this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Slokovic-Glumac, if I could address you on behalf of the Defence, since I think this relates to your witnesses. I hope that notification was given to the Defence that this is what we propose doing. As I've said, this proposal would require the consent of the parties and, of course, the consent of the accused. I very much hope that it can be resolved. This case needs to be dealt with expeditiously, and it would appear that this is one way of at least not wasting more time than necessary. The matter, of course, if you want to have time to discuss it, you shall have it, but perhaps you can help us with this: There is one witness here, as we understand; is that right, a Mr. Strukar?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. As regards the first question and continuing the trial under these circumstances, I think that my colleagues will like to address this issue through Mr. Pavkovic, who is the coordinator of our group, and I think that they are going to present their proposal. As regards the witnesses who are here, for the time being, we only have Zoran Strukar here. He is the witness that we are supposed to hear today, and tomorrow we want Plavcic and Blaz, that is to say, two witnesses, and you have said correctly that they are not in The Hague for the time being. Indeed, they are snowbound in Sarajevo, but then depending on whether they show up today or not, that is what -- the continuation of the trial will depend on whether they show up today or not, and I will be examining Mr. Strukar. Could we please have a bit of time for consultations because we did not manage to tell everyone about the information we received yesterday. There were only two of us in court, in the actual building, yesterday when this piece of information arrived, so not everybody has been notified beforehand, and I would like you to hear our joint position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Radovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Before we start consultations, we would like to acquire an additional piece of information. Actually, this pertains to the following: Is Judge Cassese seriously ill or are we only talking about a few days of absence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The position, as we understand it, is that he will be back next week. Now, as I said earlier, it's very much to be hoped that this procedure could be followed in order to save time. I think the position as far as the other witnesses are concerned is that they won't be here until next week, so we are effectively talking about one witness, but inquiries can be made. How long do you want, 20 minutes? Twenty minutes then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence hopes that Judge Cassese's health is not anything to worry about and that he will return amongst our ranks very soon. The Defence is very interested in continuing the proceedings, and in that respect, it supports what the Prosecution has said. We feel that under the newly arisen circumstances, that we can continue the examination of witnesses this week, and on Monday, we would see how the situation stands with Judge Cassese. If he does not return, we will be able to see whether we are going to continue proceedings or not. In this connection, we do feel that we could continue proceedings and examination of witnesses regarding point 1, that is to say, the general facts, apart from the fact that the Defence counsel of Mr. Papic feels that when his witnesses are called and the other Defence counsel as well, when it comes to concrete charges, that a full composition of the Trial Chamber would be advisable and that they would like proceedings to continue with a full Trial Chamber. We should also like to take note of the following: It has been the practice of this Tribunal that under circumstances of this kind, a trial be continued. But we seem to feel that there is a significant difference in this regard, and that is that the Presiding Judge is absent, which is a different case to some other cases where members of the Trial Chamber were absent, and we don't think that this is a small matter. Your Honours, that would be the stand of the Defence in view of the newly arisen situation. If I may, I should like to ask you now, as you have already given me the floor, to assess the following; that is to say, I have a question that I wanted to put to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pavkovic, before you do that, let me just deal with what you have said already. This measure is a temporary measure. Were Judge Cassese not back on Monday, and it is anticipated that he would be, then, of course, the position would have to be reviewed. We have in mind that it is the Presiding Judge who is absent, and you are right in that, and, of course, were we to get to the evidence on the other counts other than Count 1, then, of course, different circumstances might arise. But may I take it then that the accused consent to our hearing evidence by deposition and that we hear the one witness who is here and any others who can be brought this week? Could you confirm that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that, precisely as you have said, and as far as that goes, we can continue, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall make an order under Rule 71 appointing the Judges who are present as Presiding Judges for the purpose of hearing deposition evidence of the witness who is here and any other witnesses who can be brought. Before we go on, there is one matter about that, and that is that the Victims and Witnesses Unit are, I believe, waiting to hear what is decided about the witnesses who are in Sarajevo. I think our view would be that, if possible, they should be brought, but if that is impracticable, then, of course, we shall have to adjourn early. I think that would be the best way to approach it. There are problems, clearly, at the airport with the snow, there are problems in terms of time as to whether the witnesses can, in fact, physically get here or not, and I would be grateful if that message could be conveyed to the Victims and Witnesses Unit. Does anybody want to say anything about that? Yes, Mrs. Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, during the break, Mr. Vaananen from the unit was here, and he said that it is practically impossible to bring the people in today, in the course of the day, and that they would prefer them to come tomorrow with the other witnesses who will be arriving for Monday. There would be problems if they did turn up late tonight in The Hague. One of them is a serious diabetic, so this would perhaps be too much for them, and they have asked this to be borne in mind, and so perhaps Monday would be a better day for those witnesses, and if Judge Cassese does not appear, then we could continue with the presentation of evidence for those two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will hear the one witness this week and review the position on Monday, it being understood the witnesses will all be here on Monday. Mr. Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would very much like to carry on proceedings, but there is one thing that cannot be postponed, and I would like to ask you to bear with me for a few minutes. I am afraid that the question that I want to pose might turn into a problem, and I cannot solve it together in consultation with the Prosecution, so I am asking for your help in this matter. What I want to ask is the following: Last week, or the week before, the Trial Chamber made a decision according to which the Defence of Vladimir Santic, the accused, that it was to enable the Prosecutor's investigators to look into the circumstance of alibi. The Defence in that sense, in order to implement this Court decision, undertook a series of technical and organisational measures in the meantime. With the Prosecution, we discussed this matter on several occasions. We discussed the modalities in which this decision could be put into practice, and we adopted the suggestions made by the Prosecution, namely, that this discussion take place neither in the homes of the witnesses or in any official institutions, we also took into account security measures, and when we felt that we had done everything in our power to implement the Court decision and to enable the investigators to have their contacts, we informed the Prosecution in writing that on the 20th of this month, when the court adjourns, that this talk be held, this meeting be held. However, yesterday we received an answer from the Prosecution, we received their letter, in fact, informing us -- we were informed and surprised at its contents -- the following: First of all, the Prosecutor refers to security measures, and the Prosecution considers that the talks that we have envisaged for Hotel Vitez, that the Hotel Vitez is not a sufficiently safe place, and the Prosecution insists that this meeting take place in Sarajevo, and that if we do not agree to that, to that venue, he will consider us not prepared to cooperate and that he will then be against having these individuals brought before the Trial Chamber. I can understand this stand, but I don't think it is a justified one, especially as this seems to be a sort of ultimatum to the Defence which has so far done everything in its power to implement the decision, and we do not feel that this kind of resolute ultimatum is in place. We can understand, of course, the reasons put forward, and we do realise that the investigators feel a certain amount of uncertainty, but I can assure you with full responsibility that there are no objective reasons for this; that is to say, those which would justify their anxieties and which would stop them from having this meeting in Vitez, all the more so as we can do nothing further at this point in the way of organisation. I must also remind the Trial Chamber that when the Prosecution uses the term and refers to "security" and "safety," this Honourable Trial Chamber made a decision a little while ago to visit Ahmici and it did not feel in jeopardy and did not consider that security measures were something that should postpone that visit. I would also like to mention another point in this regard, and that is that we must bear in mind the interests of the witnesses themselves in the sense that they are witnesses who live in the area, and that all three of them, I think, are from Vitez, and that they do not feel secure in Sarajevo either. This Trial Chamber made a decision for the free passage of all witnesses, including these three witnesses, and this applies to their coming to court as well and spending time in the Tribunal and returning home. So we cannot accept what the Prosecution is offering. Finally, I feel that we can settle the matter in the following way; that is to say, as we agreed on in principle, to have the interview take place in Vitez or, alternatively, that the witnesses directly, prior to coming to the Trial Chamber, have a meeting with the Prosecution and enable the Prosecution investigators to hold the talks and meetings they need. I hope that you will understand the reasons for which I have had to take the floor on this issue because it is a question that we cannot settle ourselves and our time is almost up because it is a matter which takes place next week because, of course, we wish to implement in full the trial decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, before you begin, clearly we cannot make an order at the moment because the Chamber as constituted is not the Trial Chamber, but perhaps we can facilitate a resolution of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, yes. I would like to inform this Tribunal, relay a certain amount of information to this Tribunal, and perhaps allay some of the fears that Mr. Pavkovic has and to explain that the proposal made by Mr. Pavkovic is not realistic. I would like to remind Mr. Pavkovic that we are in a situation in which the Tribunal and the accused have agreed to hear the witnesses in the defence of alibi for Mr. Santic, although we are now in a very irregular situation with regards to the Rules. Notice of the defence of alibi was not respected within the time limits provided by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Nonetheless, in order to ensure that the rights of the Defence are guaranteed or are respected, the Trial Chamber agreed to hear these witnesses subject, however, to the possibility of the Prosecution meeting with these witnesses before they appear before the Trial Chamber. We sent to Mr. Pavkovic, and I believe that the Trial Chamber also received a copy of this, proposals in which these witnesses, the Defence witnesses, and Defence of Mr. Santic, these meetings were to be taking place. Mr. Santic and Mr. Pavkovic have proposed that the lawyer for Mr. Santic, in addition to a representative, be present at the interview, and that the interview be recorded and that the recording be disclosed immediately to Mr. Pavkovic. What we request, however, and I believe that the Tribunal may understand, and I hope that Mr. Pavkovic must understand this as well, is that in all serenity, in all security -- an environment of security and serenity must also be there for our investigators and for Defence witnesses. The only question which can be raised here today in relation to what Mr. Pavkovic has just stated is the question of the place in which this interview would take place. Mr. Pavkovic has requested that this meeting take place at Hotel Vitez. According to the information at our disposal and according to the information we received from SFOR located in the area of Busovaca, it is not at all appropriate that this meeting take place there for security reasons because SFOR would have to deploy a large number of measures to secure those present; it would be very difficult and very dangerous for the city of Vitez. We must also keep in mind the fact that we have to also bring in video recording equipment for this conference and that this would have to be organised with great care. Therefore, we request and we have great hopes that this meeting will take place in the Office of the Prosecutor in Sarajevo where we can have the absolute guarantee of security. I can understand that Mr. Pavkovic may doubt this, but we can also assure the transportation of the witness, if necessary, to Sarajevo, and return the witness to Vitez. We believe that this discussion about the place of meeting is unfortunate and we hope that we can come to an agreement, and we hope that Mr. Pavkovic will understand that we cannot go to Hotel Vitez with all the equipment we have need of and that it will be very necessary that this take place in Sarajevo and that there will be no inconvenience whatsoever for the Defence witness. In addition to that, we will ensure an environment of serenity in this meeting, and this will enable the debate to continue before this Tribunal in serenity as well. This is the type of response that we sent to Mr. Pavkovic. This is not an ultimatum by any reasons. This is simply a response. We hope that Mr. Pavkovic will understand our resolve on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Pavkovic, as I said earlier, in the absence of the Presiding Judge, clearly the Trial Chamber as presently constituted can make no sort of order at all. But having heard both sides, we would recommend that you try and find a compromise in this matter, that the Prosecution objections to Hotel Vitez you've heard set out, and we've heard the objections of your witnesses to going to the Office of the Prosecutor. Now, it would seem to me that this is a matter which should be resolved between the parties. It's not a matter, really, for the Trial Chamber to rule on. And we invite you to pursue the usual channels vigorously, and try to resolve the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll try and do that. We are not contesting the matter, but the road to Sarajevo and the sojourn in Sarajevo, and to ensure the protective measures that we consider the witness merits and must be the type that was afforded to the witnesses by the Tribunal. But we do, of course, accept your suggestions, Mr. President, and shall do our utmost to resolve the issue and find a compromise solution, because it is in our interest to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, is there anything else before we hear the witness? Very well. Let the witness be brought in. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you would like to sit down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Examined by Ms. Slokovic-Glumac:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please introduce yourself, tell us your name, where you were born and when?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: My name is Zoran Strukar. I was born in Vitez on the 16th of April, 1961.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which schooling have you had?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I completed secondary school in Sarajevo, the centre for cadres training of the Ministry of the Interior, which lasts for four years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, where were you employed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I was employed in the police station in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What job did you hold?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: For two or three years I worked as a policeman in town, traffic policeman, and then I worked on the ground, and then I went to a special course, to attend a special course in Sarajevo. I worked there until 1991, and then I started working as a policeman in town again until 1992, and then I also went to take another course in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please stop at this point. You said that you completed certain courses, and that that is why you worked as a signals officer, communications officer?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that implies receiving telegrams, working at the telephone exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you did these jobs in Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that in 1991, you worked as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, perhaps in mid-1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the chief of police at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: That's when elections were held, and in Vitez, it was agreed to have an appropriate allocation of jobs in keeping with the outcome of the elections. The commander of the police was a Muslim, and the chief of police was a Croat. So it was Pero Skopljak and Saban Mahmutovic, respectively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is to say the two top posts in the police were divided according to the outcome of the elections; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, according to the outcome of the elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pero Skopljak: Do you remember when he came to the post of chief of police in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. I know that these elections were held, and that is when he came in. I don't know the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it 1991? The elections were at the end of 1990, so was it 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, probably the end of 1991. I don't know. I don't know. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Saban Mahmutovic, who was commander of the police, he was a Muslim; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as regards policemen, how were policemen employed in the police? Did people pay attention to ethnic composition there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, always in terms of the numbers of the Muslim, Croat, and Serb populations, and the number of the policemen on the force was always proportionate to that. So this was a tradition from the earlier days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ethnic composition of the police basically matched the ethnic composition of the population; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. About half/half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall at that time how many policemen there were on the force in the police station in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: About 27.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of 1991, when the war had already broken out in Croatia, did something happen in relation to the police in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, nothing. Nothing really happened. People did their regular work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did something happen to the stocks of weapons held by the police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: While I was still working on communications, telegrams were coming in from Sarajevo saying that weapons from the police station should be withdrawn to Sarajevo. And the answer was that we had warehouses at the Princip factory --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Since you're already describing this, who sent this telegram to the police station in Vitez, and what was exactly stated in this telegram, and why were weapons taken away?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: The telegram arrived from Sarajevo from the Republican SUP, and the problem allegedly was that the police station did not have adequate warehouses for storing the weapons that we had, and then these weapons would have to be returned to Sarajevo. That was the alleged reason. Then the answer was that we do have an explosives factory called Princip, and it does have appropriate warehouses for this explosive that they make and that we can also store our own weapons there. However, after that, another telegram came from Sarajevo saying that regardless of that, the weapons had to be returned to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about other police stations? Did they receive the same order? Were weapons collected from all the police stations in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This was a circular telegram. Every day there were telegrams that were sent to all police stations, and it said "To All" in the heading, so everybody received the same telegrams.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the decision in response to this request, after you said that you had appropriate warehouses for these weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: The answer was that we would store these weapons at this warehouse. However, they said that they wanted the weapons returned after all. However, Pero Skopljak mobilised the reserve militia, it was called in those days, the reserve police, at various local communities. From three local communities, he got people and formed a police station. And the weapons that we had in our warehouse was given to these reserve policemen. And the town also had a reserve police station consisting of reservists, and they were also given weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in a way, this meant an activation of the reserve police force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you also said that at different local communities, he would bring various reserve police stations together; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. Before, every local community had a reserve police station of its own; but then Pero made a single police station out of three previous ones, and in this way he managed to distribute weapons to all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of weapons were distributed then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I think that every station got a sub-machine gun and also some automatic rifles, and the rest were semi-automatic rifles with ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the way in which weapons were distributed in the surrounding villages around Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in all the local communities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these weapons, is that the way that Ahmici, their local community received weapons too?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, Ahmici belonged to Nadioci. Actually these were three local communities, local communities Ahmici, Santici, and Nadioci and they covered this single police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These weapons were handed over to them at the same time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, everybody equally. They also received uniforms, I think, reserve policemen uniforms, and they were blue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember who was commander of the reserve police force in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I do remember. It was Zahid Ahmic, because I was commander of the reserve police force in Vitez, so we cooperated. We matched the numbers of the weapons, and some of the weapons were out of order and they had to be returned, so we would see each other every now and then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you say precisely when this happened, when these weapons were handed out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I think this was the end of '91 or autumn, somewhere towards the end. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. While we're on the subject of weapons, this is a bit out of context, but tell me, do you know anything about how the Territorial Defence weapons were handed out? This was the weaponry owned by the police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there were also weapons in the area of Central Bosnia that were held by the Territorial Defence, is that right, or do you know whether the arms of the Territorial Defence were taken away from them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not sure about that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, what were the weapons that were at Slimena?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: That was held by the JNA. There was a weapons warehouse. I don't know whose weapons these were, but I realised later that these were rifles and sub-machine guns, and other things, but I didn't really know who they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do not know whether these were Territorial Defence weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: That, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Then we won't go into that. Do you know how these weapons were given away, I mean, from Slimena?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: When the warehouses were liberated, I heard on the news that these weapons would be shared equally between the Muslims and the Croats. This had happened in the morning, I mean, these warehouses were taken in the morning. So the locals, the citizens, took their own cars and went to these warehouses. Some were wounded. Some of them were wounded by mines as they happened to come across them, and then Saban came across a patrol with Dzemo Bektas, Hrustanovic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. You have to bear in mind the fact that this is being interpreted, so please speak slowly. Could you please tell us this from the very beginning? Who sent who to Slimena and who had these weapons distributed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Saban Mahmutovic sent Dzemo Hrustanovic out on a patrol to regulate traffic because there was a traffic jam up there around these warehouses, and I heard later on that these weapons would be shared equally between the Muslims and the Croats. I had a meeting about this somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Saban Mahmutovic at that time was commander of the police, and this Dzemo Hrustanovic, who was he, a policeman?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, he was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was sent to Slimena to check what was going on in terms of the distribution of weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, to regulate traffic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, to regulate traffic then. Were people allowed to come with their own cars and take weapons away?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: At first, it was allowed, but afterwards, it was forbidden. However, again, there were some vehicles that managed to get in because they knew the people who were up there or whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you? You said that you went to Sarajevo for further education. This was in 1992, and I interrupted you at that point.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992, we needed two criminology technicians for the Vitez station, and Zlatko Kader (phoen) and I went there. We went to attend a course in Sarajevo, and we were there until April 1992 when the blockade of Sarajevo started. Edo and I managed to get out somehow, and we came back to Vitez and reported at our station. We reported back to work. Since then, I've been working as a criminology technician at the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was this person that was with you? What was the name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Edo Zlotrg, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he a Muslim or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: A Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He also worked with you as the criminology technician after that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you returned to Vitez in April 1992. Tell us, what was the situation like in Vitez then as regards security?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: As regards security, there was a high rate of crime. There were more burglaries, car thefts. Documents were forged. Vehicles that were stolen could not be legalised, so, therefore, the documents for these vehicles were forged so that the perpetrators of these offences would be protected from the police. Then there was also looting and robberies and arson, and people started wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just a minute, please. Could you tell me whether there was shooting in town? Were there such phenomena?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, from April onwards, there was more and more of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the point of view of security and safety, how would you assess the situation from April '92 until April '93, throughout that year?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Month after month, it became increasingly difficult to work and live there. There were many groups that had weapons. There was shooting. Explosives were thrown at various buildings, in the street. It was not safe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, you worked in the crime section of the police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, what were the reasons that led to this kind of a deterioration of the security and safety situation in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: In my opinion, the major reason for this was the fact that people wore uniforms, and the young men who wore uniforms would join the units that appeared at that time. PPNs, that's what they were called. We, as the civilian police, could not do anything about the military, and when we would come for an on-site investigation or if we were informed through various operations and if we realised that someone had done something, but then if this person would show an ID saying that he belonged to the military, then we would have to hand them over to the military, so we couldn't really do our job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that the reason for increasing the crime rate was the fact that people wore uniforms, you are actually saying that the civilian police could not intervene vis-a-vis persons in uniform; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. We were not in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, you said that in Vitez, people with weapons appeared who set up their own groups?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these groups were PPNs, you said. What does "PPN" mean?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: They called themselves PPNs --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Defence counsel is overlapping the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: These are units for special purposes, special purposes units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which way were these units organised; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: They were organised independently. One man would get a few more men, and he'd have uniforms for them. In Vitez, there was Darko Kraljevic who organised the HOS. They wore black uniforms, and later on, this HOS got a new name, Vitezovi. Young men joined this group. They were looking for glory. They wanted to prove themselves, and these people who had already carried out certain actions were there idols, and they tried to follow them. They had very short haircuts so that they would look like film stars, and they also had a lot of ammunition, and they would get drunk in restaurants and cafes. They did not observe the working hours of restaurants and cafes, which was until 10.00 or 11.00 in our town, and nobody could get them out of these cafes and restaurants. When they would get drunk, they would start shooting, and that's how others were wounded. There was material damage, and explosives were thrown. They did all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Vitezovi, you said that they were a special purposes unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was in Vitez, but every town had a unit of its own of this nature, and the PPN members respected the territory of other units. So those who were engaged in crime in Vitez did not interfere in Nova Bila and vice versa, only if there was an action which they considered to be important, such as smuggling of cars or car theft, whatever perhaps they would care about altogether because they would have a joint interest involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about in other places? You said that the Vitezovi existed in Vitez. In other places, there were other units, other special purposes units. Do you know what they were called?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: For example, in Nova Bila, I know that they were called the Zuti or yellow. This was a nickname given to their leader Andric who was nicknamed Zuti. Later on, he set up his own military police. Then we have the Tvrtkovci and the Jokeri. The Jokeri were members of the military police as an anti-terrorist unit. Then there were the Munja, the light assault unit, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any conflicts between these groups?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, there were. In Nova Bila, to quote an example, the Zuti had a conflict with the other group led by Tuka, Zoran Tuka. In that conflict, Tuka shot at the leader of the Zuti, that is to say, Zuti himself, and wounded him in the back, and he is still an invalid and has to use an invalid chair. The Zuti group, in retaliation, set up an ambush for Tuka, and they killed him in that ambush.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was a mutual settling of accounts?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why these clashes broke out? What were the interests of these groups?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Usually they were material interests, that is to say, theft and money relations, unsettled money matters. Those were the principal causes of the conflicts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In these groups, were there any out-and-out criminals?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, there were criminals in the groups with criminal records. Yes, there were. Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these units, the Vitezovi and Zuti units, the Tvrtkovci, were they involved in crime of any kind at that time already?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, they were, but we as the civilian police, even if we did know of things, were unable to undertake any action because they were the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have any weapons, and if so, what type?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They had weapons, short-barreled weapons and long rifles, and I saw some of these black rifles for the first time. They have a special handle in the middle. Darko, for example, had a rifle which was called the glycerine rifle with a short barrel and a drum where the bullets were fed into, as you would for a hunting rifle, and then he would go about shooting in town whenever he felt like it, taking potshots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were the best-armed members, they had rifles that you see --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, compared to us, yes, they were the best-armed groups.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these units go to the battlefield?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, they did, very often, as far as I know. They would go to Jajce and to Vlasic, I think, and when they would return, that's what we knew about, mostly they would shoot around town, start singing, start drinking, and then this would go on until the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of the war, that is to say, when the war had already begun, did these units take part in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They took part in manning the defence lines. If the defence line would fall, they would go there to help out, and they would also engage in some breakthrough operations and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they only at the frontline or did they go to win over territory and establish their frontlines?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: They would win over territory and establish frontlines, and if they took over a defence line, they would stay there until the morning until the trenches were dug and then, when the locals turned up, they would withdraw, and they would also withdraw sometimes before this happened but, of course, the enemy didn't realise this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that they had their commanders and that these were usually the people that formed the groups in the first place. Were they in any kind of military composition, at least some of these units? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were all separate forces. Only the Jokers perhaps. They came under the jurisdiction of the military police. But I don't know the situation very well. I do know that their members were military policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Blaskic, or the Operative Zone and Blaskic as its commander, had any influence on what the Vitezovi did? Could he order, for example, the Vitezovi or the Zuti to undertake an operation of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, he could not order this. Only perhaps in the course of the war he was able to come to an agreement of some kind with them, but he could not order them to do anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Cerkez, the Vitez Brigade? Did they act together with these units, the Vitezovi in particular; do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Perhaps they had an agreement to engage in some operation, but I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well then. Let us move on and look at the conduct of the civilian police during that time. You said that you were stopped in your work and in undertaking any action towards these individuals because they were not under your jurisdiction; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, what happened, for example, if a theft was reported or a car theft was reported or any attacks of any kind; did you investigate?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Whenever we received information that a crime had been committed, a criminal offence of any kind, we would go on site to establish what had happened and there was always somebody on duty, an official on duty, to receive complaints of this kind from civilians, and then we would decide whether the crime squad was to be called out to investigate. If they were petty offences, petty thefts, or if law and order were disturbed, then it would be the policemen who would go out to investigate; but if it was a more serious crime, like breaking and entering or any other kind of assault and battery or anything of that kind, then we would be called. Usually the perpetrators were unidentified, and we would go and collect clues and take witness statements, eyewitness statements, and so on. If a perpetrator had been identified, we would take him into custody, bring him into the police station, and if we found that he was a member of a military unit, we had to turn him over to the military police. If he was not, then we would investigate the matter, question him, and take the necessary procedure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you performed your duties to the best of your ability as far as you were able to. Did you have any forms to fill in?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I had a book, a record, a register of the crimes committed, and when we would file a criminal complaint against the perpetrators, this was recorded in a separate recordkeeping book or register.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us in what way you uncovered a very large chain of car smugglers and what the repercussions of that were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I wonder where we're going. Mrs. Glumac, I haven't stopped you so far, but we're in 1992 and we are now about to hear about an investigation as to car smuggling. Is that going to help us, really, to decide this case?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think that it is because a chain was uncovered by the civilian police, a chain of smugglers, car smugglers, and this operation ended in that all the special purposes units attacked the police station, in fact freed the perpetrators, and this is going to have links with what the witness will be saying later on. In fact, the operations undertaken by the civilian police and the way in which it tried to introduce law and order were stopped by the special purposes units, and the way they did this will be seen from the report that is going to be presented here. So this whole testimony has to do with a testimony made in the first part of the trial when it was stated that the situation was very uncertain, exclusively for the Muslims, and this testimony -- this witness is showing that the security situation was at a generally very low level and that it was unsafe and that everybody was subjected to this situation, the Muslims, the Croats, the Serbs, and the members of the different services that existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Then let us move then as quickly as possible to the attack on the police station rather than the details of any investigation, unless they're relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. I wasn't going to go into the details of this, just the results, what happened as a result. I should like to ask the usher now to distribute this document to the Trial Chamber and the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D75/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Strukar, while the document is being studied, would you tell us what knowledge you arrived at when you did your police investigating in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: We found that the young men from Novi Bila -- from Nova Bila were smuggling cars and falsifying documents, forging documents, and that we undertook an action to impound the vehicles and take into custody the perpetrators. Sveda, who was the main culprit, was taken into custody, and a group arrived at the police station from Novi Bila with three-barreled guns and a car to set Ferdo free.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There seems to be a mistranslation. Just one moment, please. So when Ferdo Gazibaric was taken into custody, who came to the police station?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: A group of Zuti came to the police station with a truck with a three-barreled gun and a bus full of its members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means the members of the special purposes unit belonging to Zuti; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: As we knew that they would be arriving, we prepared to meet them and tackle them, and when they arrived, Zuti got out, and when he saw what was being prepared, he said that there should be a negotiation, and Pasko, who was the head of the regional military police did negotiate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's Pasko's name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I think his name was Ljubicic, I'm not quite sure. He negotiated with him, and he said that an agreement had been reached, and when the police dispersed, Zuti, with a team of men, stormed the police station, bashed down all the doors, beat up the officer on duty, took the vehicle, asked where Ferdo was. He said that he was in the Kaonik camp. He went with Pasko to Kaonik camp and freed Ferdo, and they went off in the direction of Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Ferdo Gazibaric was arrested on that occasion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was actually freed from Kaonik; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the police had already taken this Ferdo Gazibaric to Kaonik as soon as he was arrested; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. As soon as he was arrested, he was taken to Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Would you please have a look at this report now? Can you tell me whether this report describes the event that you just told us about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you took part in taking Ferdo Gazibaric into custody and whether you took part in this entire affair?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I did take part in the discovery of this crime, but I did not go to Kaonik, take this person into custody. I went home after work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This report is called "Information about persons who organised the attack on the MUP and the military police in Vitez"; is that right? The persons that are mentioned in this report, do you know them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, some of them. Zarko Andric, that is Zuti.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what they were involved in?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Then this nickname Klempo, I heard that he was an arms smuggler. I watched this on television, but I did not have any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Could you please look at the last page and see who signed this report and whose seal and stamp this is? Could you tell us whether you recognise the signature and whether you recognise the seal?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: It was signed by Pasko Ljubicic. I do not know his signature, but I do know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also, was he commander of the 4th Battalion of the military police at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the stamp and seal?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: This is Herceg-Bosna, defence department. I saw similar coats of arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Tell us, were there any other such cases that you may remember? Do you remember any other cases of having the police station attacked?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Explosives were thrown, but nothing more direct than that. I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that very often at the time a lot of explosives were thrown around Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were only Muslim buildings, Muslim houses, endangered in this way, or Croat houses too?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: In addition to Muslim buildings and houses, Croatian buildings and houses were destroyed too, and Serb houses and shops as well. And for example, shops like Ogrjev, there were lootings, robberies, and goods were taken away. And also explosives were thrown if there was some kind of a conflict, and also I know that the balcony of a Croat was shot at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember any restaurants or cafes owned by Croats that were blown up at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: In town, the Kamen cafe owned by Jukic was blown up. Then also in Zabilje, also a restaurant called Tina. And then in front of various public buildings like the medical centre, the cinema, the police station. Perhaps there were other cases too, but I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there any cases of arson in the villages, do you remember, at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there was arson in Kruscica, where there is predominantly Muslim population, and weekend cottages, weekend cottages belonging to Croats and Serbs were usually torched. And also where there's a majority Croat population, Muslim weekend cottages were torched too. And also there is a Serb village, Hrasnice by Tolovici, and everybody had moved out, and then all the houses were burned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I think in '93.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did someone move into this village?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: The village of Tolovici? Yes, yes, refugees, I think, of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show you some other reports pertaining to explosives and attacks by explosives, and could you please tell us whether these were areas inhabited by Croats, Muslims, or both.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So please, could Defence Exhibit D31/2 be shown to the witness. Mr. President, please, could you bear in mind the fact that we should take a break? I've just heard from one of the accused something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we started at 9.35; we'll finish at 5 minutes past 11, and we'll take the break then, when you get to a convenient moment about then.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you had a look at this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we are talking about a report about attacks with explosives in 1993; tell me these places that are mentioned, the Red Cross, the clinic, MUP, the Crnogorka building, which areas are these, and was there only a Muslim population there, or only a Croat population, or a mixed population?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: This was in town, and all these are public institutions. Around the clinic there are two buildings where both Muslims and Croats live. Then across the street from the civilian MUP, Ministry of the Interior, there is also a building where civilians live, and the building called Crnogorka is an apartment building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we're talking about the centre of the town of Vitez, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It's all in a circle, really. Also there is a balcony here, Zoran Krizanovic's balcony. That building was called Vitezanka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Zoran Krizanovic a Croat, or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Zoran is a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether such occurrences were frequent?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, practically every evening something was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Could the usher please show the witness this official note, too?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D76/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Strukar, is this an event that you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I heard about this event, but I did not investigate it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explosives were thrown in this case, too, weren't they, at Impregnacija? What was Impregnacija?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Impregnacija was a wood processing factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also an explosive was thrown at the house of Dzemo Mujanovic which was nearby; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: It's near this enterprise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was a relatively strong explosion because --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: The glass broke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, and the house was damaged. Did the police do something when there were such explosions which obviously endangered the people who were there and who lived there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, they went to investigate. This was an on-site investigation. They tried to get fingerprints, et cetera, so if the perpetrator could be found, then this could be used as evidence, and most probably neighbours were interviewed and possible witnesses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at this official note and tell us who signed it? It is an official note of the 4th Batallion of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. It was signed by Ivan Josipovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who this person is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he do? Was he a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, he was a military policeman, and he worked in the military police in charge of operations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said that the police tried to do something, that it intervened in cases when they thought that dangerous things were being done. Later on, how was all of this processed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: A criminal report would be filed with the office of the prosecutor, which existed in Travnik before, but then it was closed down, and then it was supposed to open in Vitez and start working in Vitez, that is to say, that this criminal report would be filed with the office of the prosecutor, and then they would send it on further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did this office of the prosecutor cease to operate in Travnik, and when did this happen? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Because the roads were often blocked. I think that's the reason. I don't know exactly when it stopped working, though. I think in '93, '93, most probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, was an office of the prosecutor established in Vitez? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I heard that it was supposed to be established, and it was established eventually, but I can't remember whether it was before the war or during the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the municipal court or the district court? In the prewar days, in what jurisdiction was Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Of the municipal court. The municipal court functioned on the territory of the municipality of Vitez, and we would always call an investigating judge from Travnik, from the basic court there. For a given period of time, he operated in Travnik, and then he stopped operating, and this was also established in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the higher court? Did it exist at that time for the area of Vitez, and where was this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I think that during the war it was in Vitez, but I don't know when -- I don't know when.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This prewar period, do you remember whether the office of the prosecutor operated then? In 1993, was there an office of the prosecutor in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I cannot recall. I do not know when it ceased to operate in Travnik and when it started operating from Vitez. I do not recall the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could take a break now, as I will be moving on to a different subject in the next part, so perhaps this would be a good point to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Slokovic-Glumac, do you think you will be able to conclude your examination in time to finish this witness today? Clearly if we can do that, it would be desirable, rather than having to come back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: It depends on the Prosecutor, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Slokovic-Glumac, what we propose, in order to deal with this witness today, is that we should sit this afternoon. That would mean that we would go on now until 1.00. We would then take the luncheon adjournment until 3.00, it would have to be, and then sit between 3.00 and half past four. I hope that won't cause inconvenience to anybody, but it seems a more efficient way of dealing with the matter, rather than all having to come back tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That is agreeable with us as well, and I think that we will complete what we have with the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Strukar, let us go on to the 19th of October, 1992 because some incidents occurred there which are vital for the situation in Vitez. Would you tell us where you were on the 19th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: On the 19th of October, 1992, at the end of my work shift for the day, we were informed that there was a traffic accident in Kuber [as translated] and that some people had been killed in the accident. We informed the investigating judge and the prosecutor that we should go out on-site --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you repeat the place where the accident took place because it says "Kuber."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Klupe near Nadioci. It is a particularly dangerous curve, bending curve, bend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The place is near Nadioci and Ahmici, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went there to perform an on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. We waited for the judge and prosecutor in the police station for about half an hour, and as he failed to arrive, we went on-site to see what had actually occurred. We came to the site of the accident and waited there for a further two hours, and the public prosecutor from Travnik turned up alone and said that the others could not arrive because there was a roadblock and that we should get through the business together with him which we did and started on the return journey to Vitez. When we arrived in the vicinity of the cemetary at Topole, which is close to Ahmici, on the road, I noticed people with weapons. There were some obstacles positioned on the road which we called hedgehogs, and I drew closer because I saw a young man with a weapon coming towards us and made a sign to us to stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that? Tell the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: It was Zavid Ahmic, the commander of the reservist police unit for Ahmici. He asked me where we had been. I told him that there was an accident and that we had been there. We asked to pass by, and he said, "Yes, you can pass through but don't come back." Some of the young men removed the obstacles. I continued on my journey and came to the police station. I saw that all the lights had been turned off. This seemed a little strange. I slowed down, and in front of the building, there were two uniformed men wearing black uniforms, and they told me to stop. They gave me signs to stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. The members of which unit were positioned in front of the police station?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time, but I learned later that they were members of the Vitezovi. He asked me what my name was and my co-driver. I said his name was Zoran. And they said, "What do you want here?" And I said, "We work here." He said, "You don't work here anymore. Go home." I took one of my colleagues to Jardol. I gave him a lift because I saw that the situation was dangerous, and I, myself, returned home. I didn't stop off at the police station anymore. Half an hour later, the telephone rang and an unknown voice told me to come to the police station and to bring the official vehicle that I had been using and to bring my office keys with me and the keys to the other official vehicles. So I went to the police station. I stopped in front, and a soldier escorted me up to my own office. And through the corridor, I noticed that all the doors had been broken down and all the drawers had been ransacked. My own drawer was not ransacked. I took out my keys, and the man told me to go downstairs with him where I was awaited by his leader or chief, and I recognised him. His nickname was Sidi. He said, "Where are the keys," and I said, "Over there." And he said, "Go off home, and I don't want to see you here anymore." So I went home that evening and stayed home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody stay in the police station that day, that is to say, the 19th of October, of the policemen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I didn't see anybody. I went right round the police station because the crime squad office was at the end of the corridor, and I saw nobody along the way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go to your office at the police station the following day?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, I wondered what I was going to do during the night, and in the morning, I went to the police station to see what I was going to do. When I arrived at the police station, the young man asked me what I wanted, and I asked whether any of the policemen had come to work and whether we could take up our duties, and he said, "No. Go to the Hotel Vitez." I found some of my colleagues there, and I spent some time in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the entire police station moved to the premises of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: The Croats were moved there. The Muslims, however, set up their own police station in the Mahala in Old Vitez, Stari Vitez, in the fire brigade building. So they moved to the fire brigade building and set up their own station there. Several policemen who remained just reported for duty and said they would like to work there, and they were told to go home and that they would be called when needed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that means that there was a division in the police force after that incident; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as I was able to understand, the whole of the police station was sent away from the police station by the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: The whole police station was taken over by the Vitezovi, and nobody, none of the police force, could enter the building. Everybody was thrown out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many days did you spend in the hotel as a police force?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I think we spent about 10 to 20 days in the hotel. I'm not quite sure. I know that we were there, stationed there, for a time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Muslims, you say, formed their own police force in what they referred to as the Mahala; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. We saw that they were absent, and then we learnt that they had established their own police station in Stari Vitez, in the Mahala, in the fire brigade building there. With our chief, the commander, the chief -- their chief, Saban Mahmutovic, communicated with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Saban Mahmutovic, therefore, joined the police force set up in the Mahala; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the civilian police of the Croatian part at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: It was Pero Skopljak still, and then he tendered his resignation because of the events that happened, and then Mirko Samija took over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any problems? Was Pero Skopljak asked to resign previously by the police cadres, that is to say, by Sarajevo? Do you know whether anything like that was requested?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I don't know whether the request came from Sarajevo, but I do know that after this event took place, we asked the Muslims to have a meeting and to start working together again, and they requested, they asked as a condition for this, that Pero Skopljak tender his resignation, and then the Croats asked Saban Mahmutovic to do the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As Pero Skopljak's deputy?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, as chief of police. Pero Skopljak tendered his resignation and said, "There you are. I don't want to be an obstacle." The Muslims did not follow suit, so that we had no further contacts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether your status underwent a change, that is to say, what about your salaries and so on? Did you receive your salary from Sarajevo after that or did your salaries come to you from Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I later learned that with that date, our labour relations, that is, the Croat members of the police force, relations were severed there, and we began receiving salaries from Mostar, from the government. I don't actually know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All the Croats in Vitez, were their work duties severed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Only for the Croat policemen, members of the police force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you take a look at your work booklet, and I'd like the usher to hand around this document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D77/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you take a look at the pages that have been photocopied from the original? Tell us whether that is your own personal work booklet. Would you take a look at page 3 which states that on the 19th of October, 1992, you were relieved of your duties as of that date and that the RSUP, that is to say, the Republican SUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the security centre in Zenica told you of the fact that you would be relieved of your duties, the Vitez station. So your function ceased as of the 19th of October, 1992; you were no longer an employee of the police station. This was terminated by the SUP from Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that also the case with your colleagues, the other policemen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. When I was in Sarajevo and wanted to retrieve my work booklet, the clerk told me that I was to have received a certificate stating that I was relieved of my duties as of that date, and the clerk said -- she was a woman -- and she said that as of that date, we would be relieved of our duties. But I never saw this actually on paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The contents of your work booklet, who wrote in the contents and your years of service? Where was your booklet located?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: In the Republican SUP of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that means that that is where your years of service were recorded and everything else, the information about your employment. When the civilian police became divided up and the Muslims moved to the Mahala and the Croatian part remained in Vitez, how was the work of the police regulated?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, what we did was the following: We would work in areas where the majority of the population were Croats, whereas they worked where the majority population were Muslims. Then we would cooperate in the exchange of reports. For example, if a perpetrator was a Croat and he was on Muslim territory and had perpetrated a crime, we would take a statement down from the individual and send them that statement and report. That is the way in which we would function. We would go out for an on-site investigation, when a theft, in case of a theft or anything else, we would do this together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there was a sort of territorial division covered by both police stations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. For safety reasons, for security reasons, they would cover their own territory and we would cover ours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did this cooperation function during the on-site investigations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, when we did the investigation together, the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the areas held by the Muslim police? What area did the problems occur?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: In the Mahala of Stari Vitez, in Kruscica, Veceriska, those were the areas, perhaps in Preocica to a certain extent but to a lesser extent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the Croatian police would go on the on-site investigation, when were they called to the Mahala to perform on-site investigations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN STRUKAR
